etymology: A town on the western border of the tribe of Zebulun, named in the marking out of its bounds; the name is taken to mean “trembling” or “a steep place.”
biblical_def: Maralah was a town on the western border of Zebulun, named in the tracing of that tribe’s bounds: “And their border went up toward the sea, and Maralah, and reached to Dabbasheth” (Jos 19:11). It is nowhere else mentioned; it is a boundary-stone, a mark by which the surveyors of the inheritance drew the line of Zebulun’s portion. The rolls of the inheritance are full of such border-towns, and they preach a settled truth: the LORD Himself appoints the bounds of His people. “When the most High divided to the nations their inheritance, when he separated the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deu 32:8). The line that ran by Maralah was no accident of politics or the fortune of war; it was the boundary God had ordained, that each tribe might know its portion and be content within it. The believer reads in every such border-town the doctrine that God has set the bounds of his lot as well — his station, his measure, his place in the body of Christ — and that these lines are fallen unto him in pleasant places by a Father’s hand. To know one’s bound and to keep within it, neither coveting a neighbor’s portion nor despising one’s own, is a large part of godly contentment.
webster_summary: A border town of Zebulun; a witness that the LORD Himself appoints the bounds of His people’s inheritance.

etymology: A town on the western border of Zebulun, named in the marking out of its bounds; the name is taken to mean “a hump” or, from a kindred root, “honey” or “a place of honey.”
biblical_def: Dabbasheth was a town on the western border of Zebulun, named as the line of the tribe’s portion ran along: “And their border went up toward the sea, and Maralah, and reached to Dabbasheth, and reached to the river that is before Jokneam” (Jos 19:11). It is a boundary-town, named nowhere else. Its name is taken by some to signify a hump or rounded height, and by others, from a kindred root, a place of honey. If the sweeter sense be allowed, the little border-town may serve the reader as a token of the sweetness of the good land and of the good word of God. Canaan was a land flowing with milk and honey; and the promises and testimonies of the LORD are sweeter still: “More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psa 19:10). The believer who tastes that the Lord is gracious finds in His word a sweetness that the world cannot give, and reckons the statutes of God his songs in the house of his pilgrimage. Whatever the true force of its name, Dabbasheth stands on the border of the inheritance as one more grain in the harvest of a promise kept, and a quiet invitation to taste and see that the LORD, and His word, are good.

etymology: A town on the northern border of Zebulun, named in the marking out of its bounds; the name is taken to mean “gracious” or “favored of God.”
biblical_def: Hannathon was a town on the northern border of Zebulun, named as the surveyor’s line compassed the tribe’s portion: “And the border compasseth it on the north side to Hannathon: and the outgoings thereof are in the valley of Jiphthahel” (Jos 19:14). It is a boundary-town, named nowhere else in Scripture. Its name is compounded with the same root that gives us Hannah, Hanani, Hananiah, and John — the root of grace and favor; it means gracious, or favored of God. A town whose very name is Grace, set on the border of Zebulun, quietly preaches the doctrine that runs through the whole inheritance: that Israel possessed the land not by its own worth or might but by the free favor of God. “For they got not the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them: but thy right hand, and thine arm…because thou hadst a favour unto them” (Psa 44:3). It was grace that gave the land, grace that kept it, grace that named a town upon its border. And it is grace, first to last, that gives the believer his portion in Christ: chosen by grace, called by grace, kept by grace, and glorified by grace, that the whole inheritance might be to the praise of the glory of His grace. Hannathon is a small standing witness that all the good God’s people have is of His unmerited favor.

etymology: A town on the border of Zebulun and Issachar, at the foot of Mount Tabor, afterward given to the Levites; the name is taken to mean “pasture” or, from a kindred root, “word” or “speech.”
biblical_def: Daberath was a town at the foot of Mount Tabor, on the border of Zebulun and Issachar, named in the tracing of Zebulun’s bounds: “and goeth out to Daberath, and goeth up to Japhia” (Jos 19:12). It was afterward set apart from Issachar to the Levites as one of their dwelling-cities: “out of the tribe of Issachar, Kishon with her suburbs, Dabareh with her suburbs” (Jos 21:28). The name is taken by some to mean pasture, and by others, from a kindred root, word or speech. Both senses befit a Levitical town, for the Levites were the shepherds and teachers of Israel, appointed to feed the flock with the word of God. “For the priest’s lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7). A pasture-town given to the teaching tribe preaches the ministry of the word: the people of God are fed not with the husks of man’s wisdom but with the pure milk and strong meat of the Scriptures, and the ministers of God are set among them to break that bread. Where the word is faithfully taught, the flock is fed and thrives; where it is withheld or corrupted, the people perish for lack of knowledge. Daberath, the pasture of the word, witnesses that the teaching of Scripture is the appointed food of the soul.

etymology: A town in the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar, named in the roll of its cities; the name is taken to mean “two pits” or “two wells,” from wells dug there.
biblical_def: Hapharaim was a town in the inheritance of Issachar, named at the head of that tribe’s cities: “And Hapharaim, and Shion, and Anaharath” (Jos 19:19). It is named nowhere else. The name is taken to mean two pits or two wells, likely from wells or cisterns dug in that place — a fitting name in a land where water was life and the digging of a well was the work of patient faith and labor. The pit and the well are rich figures in Scripture. The pit is the emblem of trouble, of the grave, of the depths of affliction from which the soul cries to God; the well is the emblem of refreshing, of the grace that springs up to life. The psalmist joins them in his song of deliverance: “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings” (Psa 40:2). A town named for its pits or wells may remind the believer of both: that God suffers His people to be brought low into the pit, and that He is mighty to draw them up and set them on the rock; and that from Him, the fountain of living waters, spring the wells of salvation from which His people draw with joy. Whether the name look to the pit of trouble or the well of grace, it points to the God who both humbles and lifts up.

etymology: A town in the inheritance of the tribe of Issachar, named in the roll of its cities; the name is taken to mean “a gorge” or “a narrow pass.”
biblical_def: Anaharath was a town in the inheritance of Issachar, named with its neighbors: “And Hapharaim, and Shion, and Anaharath” (Jos 19:19). It is named nowhere else, a town likely set at or named for a narrow gorge or defile in the hills of Issachar. If the name indeed signify a narrow pass, it may serve the reader as a meditation on one of the Lord’s most solemn sayings, that the way of life is a narrow way. “Enter ye in at the strait gate…because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Mat 7:13-14). The road to destruction is broad, and the crowd streams down it; but the way to life is a narrow pass, hemmed in on either hand by the commandments of God, and travelled by few. This narrowness is not the meanness of a grudging religion but the safety of a guarded road: the walls that hem the way are the walls that keep the traveller from the precipice. A town named for a narrow pass reminds the believer to seek the strait gate, to walk the fenced and narrow road of obedience, and not to be carried along with the multitude on the broad way. Few find it; but he that endureth to the end, walking the narrow pass with Christ who is the way, shall come at last to the city of life.

etymology: A town in the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, afterward given to the Levites; called Mishal in Joshua’s list of Levitical cities. The name is taken to mean “asking” or “place of prayer.”
biblical_def: Misheal was a town in the inheritance of Asher, along the coastlands toward Carmel: “And Alammelech, and Amad, and Misheal; and reacheth to Carmel westward” (Jos 19:26). It was afterward set apart from Asher to the Levites as one of their dwelling-cities, where it is spelled Mishal: “out of the tribe of Asher, Mishal with her suburbs” (Jos 21:30). The name is taken to mean asking, or place of prayer, from the root of asking and petition. A Levitical town whose very name is Asking preaches the great privilege and duty of prayer, and it is fitting that such a town should belong to the tribe set apart for the service of God. The Lord Himself has bound His giving to His people’s asking: “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you” (Mat 7:7). We have not because we ask not; and the throne of grace stands open, that we may come boldly and obtain mercy and find grace to help in time of need. A town named Asking, given to the ministers of God, is a standing summons to a life of prayer: to ask of the Father in the name of the Son, and to receive, that our joy may be full. Prayer is the appointed means by which the God who has ordained the end has ordained also that His people shall seek and obtain it.

etymology: A stream or river on the southern border of the tribe of Asher, near Mount Carmel; the name is taken to mean “the black (or turbid) stream of Libnath,” or “glass-river,” perhaps from the sand at its mouth.
biblical_def: Shihor-libnath was a stream marking part of the southern border of Asher, near Mount Carmel where it ran down to the sea: the border of Asher “reacheth to Carmel westward, and to Shihorlibnath” (Jos 19:26). The name is taken to mean the black or turbid stream of Libnath, or, by another reading, glass-river, perhaps from the fine sand at its mouth from which glass was anciently made. It is a boundary-water, the natural line God set between Asher’s portion and its neighbors. Rivers and streams in Scripture are often the appointed bounds of peoples and the pictures of God’s provision; and a river of the good land turns the mind to the greater river of grace. “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God, the holy place of the tabernacles of the most High” (Psa 46:4). That river is the ever-flowing grace and presence of God among His people, a stream that no drought can dry and no enemy can stop. Shihor-libnath, a modest border-brook running to the sea, stands in the record as one of the natural gifts of the good land; and it points, past itself, to the river of the water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb, whereof the redeemed shall drink for ever.

A border-brook of the good land points to the greater river whose streams make glad the city of God — the ever-flowing grace and presence of the Most High, and at last the river of the water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb.
roots_summary: A border stream of Asher near Carmel; a natural gift of the good land, pointing to the river of God’s grace.

etymology: A town on the border of the tribe of Asher, named in the marking out of its bounds; the name is taken to mean “moved of God” or “dwelling of God.”
biblical_def: Neiel was a town on the border of Asher, named as the surveyor’s line turned toward the sunrising: the border “turneth toward the sunrising to Bethdagon, and reacheth to Zebulun, and to the valley of Jiphthahel toward the north side of Beth-emek, and Neiel” (Jos 19:27). It is a boundary-town, named nowhere else. The name is compounded with the name of God, and is taken by some to mean moved of God, and by others dwelling of God. If the former, it preaches the truth that God’s people are moved and led by Him: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God” (Rom 8:14). The believer does not order his own steps; the LORD directeth his going, moving him by His Spirit and His providence along the path of life. If the latter sense be preferred, dwelling of God, then the town speaks of the great mystery that God is pleased to dwell with men: He who inhabiteth eternity dwells also with the humble and contrite, and His people are His temple. Either way, the little border-town of Asher carries the name of God upon it, a witness that the people of God are known by His name, moved by His hand, and made the dwelling of His presence. To be moved of God and to be indwelt by God is the whole blessedness of the saint.

corruption_paragraphs: Neiel faces no postmodern redefinition. The truth its name carries answers the autonomous spirit that reckons a man the master of his own steps, owing his movements and his dwelling to none, and knowing nothing of being led or indwelt by God.

etymology: A town on the border of Asher; also the name Hiram of Tyre gave in contempt to a district of twenty cities Solomon ceded to him — “the land of Cabul.” The name is taken to mean “good for nothing” or “displeasing.”
biblical_def: Cabul was a town on the border of Asher, in the region of Galilee toward Tyre, named in the tracing of that tribe’s bounds (Jos 19:27). Its name became famous in a telling exchange between Solomon and Hiram king of Tyre. Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee in payment for timber and gold; but “when Hiram came out from Tyre to see the cities which Solomon had given him…they pleased him not. And he said, What cities are these which thou hast given me, my brother? And he called them the land of Cabul” (1Ki 9:12-13), a name understood to mean good-for-nothing, or displeasing. The proud Tyrian merchant, valuing all things by their commercial worth, despised the cities as a poor payment. Yet this same Galilee, so despised by Hiram as good-for-nothing, was the very region where, centuries later, the Light of the world would walk and preach, and where the Sun of righteousness would arise: “Galilee of the nations. The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light”. So Cabul rebukes the worldly eye that prices everything by profit and despises what God will glorify. The things which men count good-for-nothing, God is pleased to choose and to honor; the despised land of Cabul became the cradle of the gospel’s dawn. Let no believer despise what God esteems, nor esteem only what the world counts gain.

corruption_summary: A town of Scripture whose name means “good-for-nothing”; it rebukes the worldly eye that prices all by profit and despises what God is pleased to glorify.
corruption_paragraphs: Cabul names a live and abiding corruption: the worldly valuation that prices every thing, and every person, by its commercial or useful worth, and despises as good-for-nothing whatever yields no gain. Hiram the merchant looked on the cities of Galilee and saw only poor payment; the same eye today despises the weak, the small, the unprofitable, and the things of God.

Scripture answers with the choosing of God. “God hath chosen…things which are despised…yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are” (1Co 1:28). The despised land of Cabul became the very country of Christ’s ministry, where the great light dawned on them that sat in darkness. Let no believer despise what God esteems, nor esteem only what the world counts gain; for God is pleased to glorify what men count good-for-nothing.
